tips.title: Carbon dioxide plus water, with light
tips.body: $\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \rightarrow \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$, needing light and chlorophyll. Writing it the other way round is **respiration**, which is a different equation and a guaranteed lost mark.

tips.title: Which factor is limiting?
tips.body: On a graph, the factor that is limiting is the one being **changed** while the curve is still rising. Once it levels off, something **else** has become limiting: usually temperature or carbon dioxide.

tips.title: Say which factor, not just that it levels off
tips.body: "The plant cannot photosynthesise any faster" earns nothing. Name the new limiting factor: "light is no longer limiting, so the rate is now limited by the carbon dioxide concentration".

tips.title: The plateau names a different factor
tips.body: Where a graph **rises**, the factor on the x-axis is limiting. Where it **flattens**, that factor no longer is — so **something else** has become limiting, and the mark is for naming which. Read the shape first, then say which factor each part belongs to.

why.matters:
Almost every living thing on the planet is running on sunlight that a plant caught. Photosynthesis is the reaction that does the catching — it builds food out of carbon dioxide and water — and everything that eats, eats something that traces back to it.

The **limiting factor** idea is the other half, and it is the one that transfers. At any moment one thing is in shortest supply and is holding the rate down, so nothing else you improve will help until you fix that one. That is true of a greenhouse, a factory and a revision timetable.

examples.title: Why a greenhouse is worth paying for
examples.body:
A commercial grower controls three things at once: lamps for **light**, heating for **temperature**, and burners or cylinders to raise the **carbon dioxide** above the 0.04% in ordinary air.

That is the limiting factor idea used as a business. Raising a factor that is not limiting is money wasted, so the skill is knowing which one is holding the rate down now — and the answer changes through the day. Light limits at dawn; by noon on a bright day it is usually the carbon dioxide.

visual.alt: Two curves of rate against light intensity that rise together while light is limiting and then level off at different heights, the lower one where carbon dioxide is in shorter supply

examples.title: Why moving the lamp back a little changes a lot
examples.body:
In the pondweed practical the lamp is moved and the bubbles are counted, and the light does **not** fall in proportion to the distance. It falls with the **square** of it, because the same light is spread over an area and area grows as a square.

So at 20 cm the pondweed gets **a quarter** of the light it had at 10 cm, and at 40 cm it gets **a sixteenth**. A measurement taken 5 cm out of position is not slightly wrong — which is why the distance is measured to the lamp rather than estimated.

props.caption: Light reaching the pondweed, against the distance to the lamp

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion showing the light reaching the pondweed at ten, twenty and forty centimetres from the lamp: full, a quarter and a sixteenth, because intensity falls with the square of the distance

examples.title: Everything a plant is, it built out of air
examples.body:
The mass of a tree does not come out of the soil. It comes out of the **air** — carbon dioxide, joined to water, using light — and the glucose that results is the raw material for everything else the plant does.

Some is respired immediately for energy. Some is stored as **starch**, which is insoluble and so does not upset the plant's water balance. Some becomes **cellulose**, which is the plant's own walls and therefore most of its bulk. And with nitrates from the soil it becomes proteins. Wood is, in the end, air.

boxes.title: Respiration
boxes.body: Used straight away, to release energy.

boxes.title: Starch
boxes.body: Insoluble, so it stores well without upsetting water balance.

boxes.title: Cellulose
boxes.body: Built into cell walls: the plant itself.

boxes.title: Proteins and oils
boxes.body: With nitrates from the soil, for growth and seeds.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading what the glucose becomes: respired for energy, stored as insoluble starch, built into cellulose cell walls, or turned into proteins and oils with nitrates from the soil

steps.title: Plants make their own food
steps.body:
Plants, algae and some bacteria are **producers**: they make their own food from carbon dioxide and water using light. Everything else eats them, or eats something that ate them, so almost all the **biomass** on Earth starts with photosynthesis. Biomass is the mass of living material: a producer builds it from carbon dioxide and water, and every consumer in a food chain lives on biomass that a plant made.

**Photosynthesis** happens in the **chloroplasts**, which contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and the plant uses it to build glucose:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

$$6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$$

It is **endothermic**: energy is taken in from the surroundings, as light, and ends up stored in the glucose.

visuals.alt: A cross-section of a leaf showing the palisade cells packed with chloroplasts near the top surface

check.prompt: Which statement about photosynthesis is correct?
check.solution: Light energy in, glucose and oxygen out.
options: It is endothermic and takes in light energy
It is exothermic and gives out heat
It produces carbon dioxide
It happens in the mitochondria

steps.title: What the glucose is for
steps.body: Some glucose is used straight away in **respiration** to release energy. The rest is turned into other things: **starch** to store (it is insoluble, so it does not upset the water balance of the cell), **cellulose** for cell walls, **lipids** for storage in seeds, and, with **nitrate ions** from the soil, **amino acids** for proteins. That is why a plant needs minerals as well as light.

visuals.problem: Why does a plant store starch rather than glucose?

steps.text: Glucose is soluble: a cell full of it would draw in water by osmosis
Starch is insoluble, so it can be stored without affecting the water balance
When the plant needs energy, starch is broken back down into glucose

check.prompt: Which substance does a plant need from the soil to make proteins from glucose?
check.solution: Proteins contain nitrogen. Glucose has none, so the plant takes in nitrates through its roots.
options: Carbon dioxide
Chlorophyll
Nitrate ions
Oxygen

steps.title: Limiting factors
steps.body:
The rate of photosynthesis depends on **light intensity**, **carbon dioxide concentration**, and **temperature**. At any moment one of them is in shortest supply and is holding the rate back: the **limiting factor**. Increase that one and the rate rises. Increase any other and nothing happens.

On the graph, the rising part shows light limiting the rate. The flat part shows that light is no longer limiting: adding more light does nothing, because something else, carbon dioxide or temperature, has taken over as the limit.

visuals.alt: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity: the curve rises steeply, then levels off flat

check.prompt: On the flat part of a rate against light intensity graph, what would increase the rate?
check.solution: When light is not limiting, one of the other factors is.
options: Increasing the carbon dioxide concentration or the temperature
Increasing the light intensity even further than before
Nothing, because the plant is already at its maximum rate
Moving the lamp further away so the leaf is not heated

steps.title: How the factors interact
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* Draw the light graph twice, once at a **high carbon dioxide** concentration and once at low. Both curves start together, because light limits both. The low carbon dioxide curve levels off first, and lower, because carbon dioxide runs short sooner. The high curve climbs further before something else, usually **temperature**, limits it.

**Temperature** is different from the other two: photosynthesis is controlled by **enzymes**. Warming speeds them up to an **optimum**, then above about 40 °C they **denature** and the rate collapses.

The same pairing works for temperature. Draw rate against light intensity at 15 °C and at 25 °C. Both rise together at low light, because light is limiting. The 15 °C curve levels off first and lower: once light is plentiful, the enzymes are working as fast as they can at that temperature, so temperature becomes the limiting factor. Warm the plant to 25 °C and the enzymes work faster, so the rate can climb further before something else limits it.

visuals.alt: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two carbon dioxide concentrations: the higher concentration levels off at a higher rate
Rate of photosynthesis against temperature: rises to an optimum, then falls steeply as enzymes denature
Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two temperatures: both curves rise together, but the cooler one levels off first and at a lower rate

check.prompt: Two rate against light intensity curves are drawn, one at 0.04% carbon dioxide and one at 0.1%. Which is correct?
check.solution: More carbon dioxide means it stops being the limiting factor until a higher rate.
options: The 0.04% curve levels off at a higher rate, because there is less carbon dioxide to use up
The 0.1% curve starts higher at zero light, because carbon dioxide can replace light energy
The 0.1% curve levels off at a higher rate, because carbon dioxide limits the rate later
The curves are identical throughout, because light is the only factor that affects the rate

steps.title: Core practical 6.5: light intensity and rate
steps.body:
This is core practical 6.5. One version uses **pondweed** (Elodea or Cabomba) in a beaker of water with **sodium hydrogencarbonate** solution, which supplies carbon dioxide. A lamp is placed at a measured **distance**, and the bubbles of oxygen from the cut stem are **counted for one minute**. Move the lamp, wait, repeat.

The specification's own method uses **algal balls** (algae set in jelly beads) in **hydrogencarbonate indicator**. As the algae photosynthesise they remove carbon dioxide, and the indicator changes from orange-red to purple. Place tubes of algal balls at different distances from the lamp and time how long the colour change takes at each, or compare the colour after a set time against a colour chart. The shorter the time, the faster the rate: rate = 1 ÷ time.

**Sources of error**: the lamp heats the water as well as lighting it; bubbles differ in size, so a count is not a volume; light from windows and other lamps adds to the lamp's light; and judging a colour change by eye is subjective.

steps.text: Independent variable: distance from the lamp (this sets the light intensity)
Dependent variable: bubbles of oxygen per minute, or better, the volume of gas collected
Control variables: temperature (water bath or a heat shield between lamp and beaker), carbon dioxide (same sodium hydrogencarbonate solution), the same piece of pondweed
Repeat each distance three times and take a mean; give the pondweed a minute to settle after each move

props.title: Two ways to measure the rate

visuals.alt: A table of two ways to measure the rate of photosynthesis: pondweed, counting bubbles or measuring gas per minute, and algal balls, timing the indicator turning purple and taking one over the time

check.prompt: In the pondweed experiment, what is the dependent variable?
check.solution: You change the distance and measure the bubbles.
options: The volume of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution
The distance of the lamp
The number of bubbles per minute
The temperature of the water

steps.title: The inverse square law
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* Moving a lamp away does not reduce the light in proportion to the distance. Light spreads out over an area, and area grows with distance **squared**. So:

$$\text{light intensity} \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$$

Double the distance and the intensity drops to a **quarter**. Treble it and the intensity is a **ninth**. Drag the slider to see the curve.

visuals.fallback: Relative light intensity is 100 at 10 cm, 25 at 20 cm, about 11 at 30 cm, and about 6 at 40 cm.

visuals.problem: The lamp is moved from 15 cm to 30 cm. What happens to the light intensity?

steps.text: So the intensity is a quarter of what it was

check.prompt: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 30 cm from a plant. The light intensity becomes
check.solution: Three times the distance: divide by 3² = 9.
options: one third of what it was
one ninth of what it was
three times what it was
one sixth of what it was

steps.title: Your turn: predicting the rate
steps.body: *(Higher tier only.)* While light is the limiting factor, the rate of photosynthesis is proportional to light intensity, which is proportional to $1/d^2$. So you can predict a rate at a new distance by scaling with $(d_1/d_2)^2$.

visuals.problem: At 10 cm the pondweed gives 40 bubbles per minute. Predict the rate at 20 cm.

steps.text: Distance doubles, so intensity is divided by 4
10 bubbles per minute, as long as light is still the limiting factor

check.prompt: At 10 cm the pondweed gives 45 bubbles per minute. Predict the rate at 30 cm, assuming light stays the limiting factor.
check.solution: Three times the distance: divide by 9. 45 ÷ 9 = 5.

steps.title: Going deeper: reading the graph like an examiner
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* The top questions give you a graph and ask you to **explain its shape**. Say which factor is limiting on each part, and why the curve levels off where it does: the flat part is set by whichever factor is in shortest supply. When two curves are drawn, say what is the same about them (the rising part: light limiting) and what is different (the plateau: the other factor).

The second grade 9 move is plotting rate against **$1/d^2$** instead of distance. Because light intensity is proportional to $1/d^2$, a **straight line through the origin** shows that rate is directly proportional to light intensity. If the line bends over at high $1/d^2$, another factor has become limiting.

visuals.alt: Rate of photosynthesis against 1 over distance squared: a straight line through the origin, with a dashed line that follows it and then bends over and flattens

visuals.problem: Rate at 10 cm is 36 bubbles per minute. At what distance would you expect 4 bubbles per minute?

steps.text: 36 ÷ 4 = 9, so the intensity must be a ninth
A ninth of the intensity means three times the distance

check.prompt: Rate is plotted against 1/d². The line is straight through the origin at first, then bends and becomes flat. What does the flat part show?
check.solution: A straight line means rate ∝ light. When it flattens, more light does nothing: something else limits.
options: The inverse square law no longer applies once the lamp is very close
The pondweed has stopped photosynthesising because its enzymes are denatured
The lamp has been switched off, so the light intensity has fallen to zero
Light is no longer the limiting factor; carbon dioxide or temperature is

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts. Endothermic.
- Producers make the biomass that every food chain depends on.
- Limiting factors: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature. The flat part of a graph is set by whichever is in shortest supply.
- Temperature has an optimum: above it, enzymes denature.
- Core practical 6.5: algal balls or pondweed at measured distances from a lamp; time for the indicator to turn purple, or bubbles or gas volume per minute; control temperature and carbon dioxide.
- Light intensity ∝ 1/d²: double the distance, a quarter of the light.

visuals.alt: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity: the curve rises steeply, then levels off flat

questions.prompt: Which are the reactants of photosynthesis?
questions.solution: Carbon dioxide and water go in; glucose and oxygen come out.
options: Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and glucose
Oxygen and water
Carbon dioxide and water

questions.prompt: Name the gas produced by photosynthesis.
questions.solution: Oxygen. It is released through the stomata, and it is what you count as bubbles from pondweed.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis is described as endothermic. What does this mean?
questions.solution: Endothermic means energy is taken in. Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and stored in glucose.
options: It takes in energy from the surroundings, here as light
It gives out energy to the surroundings as heat
It only happens at high temperatures
It needs no energy at all

questions.prompt: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.solution: Chloroplasts hold the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs the light.
options: In the nucleus, which contains the DNA
In the chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll
In the mitochondria, which release energy
In the cell wall, which is made of cellulose

questions.prompt: A graph of the rate of photosynthesis against light intensity rises and then levels off. Why does it level off?
questions.solution: On the flat part, more light makes no difference, so light is no longer the limiting factor. Something else is.
options: Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is now limiting the rate
The plant has used up all of its chlorophyll, so it cannot absorb any more of the light energy
The light intensity has stopped increasing, so the rate of photosynthesis has stopped rising too
The plant has made all the glucose it can hold, so it stops photosynthesising until some is used

questions.prompt: As temperature rises above about 40 °C, the rate of photosynthesis falls quickly. Why?
questions.solution: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled. Above the optimum, the active sites change shape and the reactions stop.
options: The plant runs out of water, because it all evaporates at high temperatures
Carbon dioxide stops dissolving in the leaf when the water is warm
Light cannot pass through warm air, so less reaches the chloroplasts
The enzymes that control photosynthesis are denatured, so they stop working

questions.prompt: Pondweed gives off 36 bubbles of oxygen in 3 minutes. Calculate the rate of photosynthesis in bubbles per minute.
questions.solution: Rate = number ÷ time = 36 ÷ 3 = 12 bubbles per minute.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed.
questions.solution: The marks are for the variables: what you change, what you measure and how, what you keep the same, and repeats.

markScheme.description: Change the distance of the lamp
Count bubbles or measure gas volume in a fixed time

criteria.text: Place the lamp at a measured distance from the pondweed and change the distance (independent variable)
Count the bubbles of oxygen in a fixed time, or collect the gas and measure its volume (dependent variable)
Keep temperature constant with a water bath or a heat shield, and keep carbon dioxide constant by using the same sodium hydrogencarbonate solution
Repeat at each distance and calculate a mean

questions.modelAnswer: Put a piece of pondweed in a beaker of water with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, which supplies carbon dioxide. Place a lamp at a measured distance, wait for the pondweed to settle, then count the bubbles of oxygen released in one minute. Repeat the count three times and take a mean. Move the lamp to a new distance and repeat. Keep the temperature the same using a water bath, or a beaker of water between the lamp and the pondweed as a heat shield, and use the same piece of pondweed and the same solution throughout.

questions.prompt: A lamp 20 cm from pondweed gives 48 bubbles per minute. Predict the rate when the lamp is moved to 40 cm, assuming light is the limiting factor throughout.
questions.solution: Doubling the distance divides the light intensity by 2² = 4. Rate is proportional to light intensity, so 48 ÷ 4 = 12 bubbles per minute.

markScheme.description: 48 ÷ 4, because doubling the distance gives a quarter of the intensity

questions.prompt: A lamp is 25 cm from a plant. Calculate 1/d², where d is the distance in cm. Give your answer as a decimal to 2 significant figures.

A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed at increasing light intensities, once in water with a low carbon dioxide concentration and once with a high concentration. Both graphs rise and then level off, but the high carbon dioxide graph levels off at a higher rate. Explain the shapes of the graphs.
questions.solution: Level-marked. The link is: the flat part of a curve is set by whichever factor is in shortest supply.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about limiting factors and the two curves, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of limiting factors and the two curves with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of limiting factors and the two curves using the correct terms

criteria.text: At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor, so increasing it increases the rate
The two curves are the same at first because light, not carbon dioxide, is limiting
The curve levels off when another factor becomes limiting
For the low concentration curve, carbon dioxide is the limiting factor on the flat part
With more carbon dioxide, the rate can rise further before something else limits it
The high concentration curve eventually levels off because temperature (or another factor) is now limiting

questions.modelAnswer: At low light intensities both curves rise together because light is the limiting factor: more light means more energy for photosynthesis, and the carbon dioxide concentration makes no difference yet. Each curve levels off when light is no longer limiting. For the low carbon dioxide curve, the flat part is set by the shortage of carbon dioxide. Adding more carbon dioxide removes that limit, so the high concentration curve keeps rising to a higher rate. It eventually levels off too, because another factor, most likely temperature, becomes limiting.

questions.prompt: Why is sodium hydrogencarbonate solution added to the water in the pondweed experiment?
questions.solution: Water on its own holds little carbon dioxide. The solution keeps the supply high so that the variable you are testing, light, is the one that limits the rate.

markScheme.description: Source of carbon dioxide, so it is not limiting

options: It makes the oxygen bubbles larger, so they are easier to see and count accurately
It provides the oxygen that the pondweed releases, so bubbles form more quickly
It releases carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide does not become the limiting factor
It keeps the water at a constant temperature, so temperature is not a limiting factor

questions.prompt: A student counts bubbles from pondweed to measure the rate of photosynthesis. Give two problems with this method and, for each, an improvement.
questions.solution: Evaluation marks are for the specific flaw in this method, then a fix that deals with that flaw.

markScheme.description: Heat shield, water bath, or LED lamp

criteria.text: Bubbles are different sizes, so counting them does not measure the volume of oxygen
Improve by collecting the gas in an inverted measuring cylinder or a gas syringe and measuring its volume
The lamp heats the water, so temperature is not controlled
Improve by using a heat shield (a beaker of water between lamp and pondweed) or a water bath, or an LED lamp

questions.modelAnswer: Counting bubbles assumes they are all the same size, but they are not, so the count is not a true measure of the volume of oxygen. Collecting the gas in an inverted measuring cylinder or a gas syringe and measuring the volume would fix this. Also, the lamp warms the water as it is moved closer, so temperature changes as well as light intensity. Putting a beaker of water between the lamp and the pondweed as a heat shield, using a water bath, or using an LED lamp that gives out little heat keeps temperature constant.

questions.prompt: A student plots the rate of photosynthesis against 1/d², where d is the distance from the lamp. The points lie on a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
questions.solution: Light intensity ∝ 1/d². A straight line through the origin against 1/d² means rate ∝ light intensity: light was limiting throughout.

markScheme.description: Rate directly proportional to light intensity

options: Temperature was the limiting factor throughout, because the line is straight rather than curved
The rate is inversely proportional to light intensity, because 1/d² falls as the lamp is moved closer
The rate does not depend on the distance from the lamp, because the line passes through the origin
The rate is directly proportional to light intensity, because light intensity is proportional to 1/d²

questions.prompt: When the carbon dioxide concentration was increased, the rate of photosynthesis rose from 8 to 14 bubbles per minute. Calculate the percentage increase.
questions.solution: Increase = 14 − 8 = 6. Percentage increase = 6 ÷ 8 × 100 = 75%.

questions.prompt: Photosynthetic organisms are described as the main producers of biomass. Which statement explains why?
questions.solution: Producers make biomass from simple molecules using light energy. Consumers cannot; they only pass on biomass that a producer made.

markScheme.description: Build biomass from CO₂ and water; consumers depend on it

options: They are the largest organisms in any habitat, so they contain more biomass than all the animals put together
They build biomass from carbon dioxide and water using light, and every other organism gets its biomass by eating them or eating something that ate them
They can respire without oxygen, so they keep growing and adding biomass when other organisms cannot
They absorb ready-made biomass from the soil through their roots and pass it up the food chain to consumers

questions.prompt: Complete the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → ___ + 6O₂. Give the missing formula.
questions.solution: Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. Six carbons from six CO₂, twelve hydrogens from six H₂O.

questions.prompt: Algal balls (algae set in jelly beads) are put in tubes of hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is orange-red at the start. One tube is placed 10 cm from a lamp and another 20 cm away. The indicator turns purple after 6 minutes at 10 cm and after 24 minutes at 20 cm. Which explanation is correct?
questions.solution: The indicator responds to carbon dioxide: it turns purple as carbon dioxide is removed from the water. **Nearer the lamp the algae photosynthesise faster, removing carbon dioxide sooner**, so the change takes 6 minutes instead of 24. The rate at 10 cm is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 times the rate at 20 cm, as the inverse square law predicts for half the distance.

markScheme.description: Nearer the lamp the algae photosynthesise faster, removing carbon dioxide sooner

options: Nearer the lamp the algae respire faster, so more carbon dioxide turns it purple sooner
Nearer the lamp the algae photosynthesise faster, removing carbon dioxide sooner
Nearer the lamp the indicator is heated more, and heat alone turns it purple
Nearer the lamp the algae release oxygen faster, and oxygen turns it purple

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction. What is the source of the energy it takes in?
questions.solution: **Light.** Photosynthesis uses light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts, to react carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen. Water and carbon dioxide are the reactants, not the energy source, and the soil supplies water and mineral ions, not heat for the reaction. The light energy ends up stored as chemical energy in the glucose.
options: Heat energy from the soil surrounding the roots of the plant
Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts
Chemical energy stored in the water taken up by the roots
Chemical energy stored in the carbon dioxide from the air

questions.prompt: A commercial grower pumps extra carbon dioxide into a greenhouse on bright, warm days, but not on dull days. Why?
questions.skill: carbon dioxide as a limiting factor
questions.solution: **Carbon dioxide is only worth adding when it is the limiting factor.** The rate of photosynthesis is held down by whichever factor is in shortest supply. On a bright, warm day light and temperature are plentiful, so the rate is limited by the carbon dioxide concentration of the air, and adding more raises the rate and the crop. On a dull day light intensity is the limiting factor: however much carbon dioxide is available, the plants cannot use it faster, so the gas would be wasted. Plants respire all the time, light does not destroy carbon dioxide, and carbon dioxide enters leaves at any temperature a plant can grow at.

markScheme.description: on bright warm days carbon dioxide is the limiting factor; on dull days light is, so extra carbon dioxide would not raise the rate

options: Light is not limiting on bright warm days, so carbon dioxide becomes the limiting factor; on dull days light limits the rate, so more carbon dioxide would not help
Carbon dioxide can only enter a leaf through the stomata when the temperature is above 30 °C, so on dull cool days any gas pumped in would stay in the air unused and be wasted
On dull days the plants respire instead of photosynthesising, so they make their own carbon dioxide and need none to be added until the sun comes out again
Bright light breaks carbon dioxide down into carbon and oxygen in the air, so on sunny days more has to be pumped in to replace what the light destroys

questions.prompt: A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed at increasing light intensities, once at 15 °C and once at 25 °C, with plenty of carbon dioxide both times. At low light intensities the two curves lie on top of each other. At high light intensities both level off, but the 25 °C curve levels off at twice the rate of the 15 °C curve. Which statement explains these shapes?
questions.skill: the interaction of light and temperature
questions.solution: **Light limits at first; temperature limits later.** At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor whatever the temperature, so warming the water makes no difference and the two curves coincide. Once light is plentiful, the rate is held by how fast the enzymes of photosynthesis can work, and that depends on temperature: at 25 °C they work faster than at 15 °C, so the curve can climb further before it levels off. Carbon dioxide was plentiful, so it was not the limit; cold water holds more dissolved gas than warm water, not less; 25 °C is well below the temperature at which the enzymes denature; and temperature affects enzyme activity at every temperature, which is why the plateaus differ.

markScheme.description: light limits at low intensity at both temperatures; at high intensity temperature limits, and enzymes work faster at 25 °C

options: At low light intensity the plant at 25 °C cannot photosynthesise any faster because the warmth denatures its enzymes before the light can be used, so the two only differ in bright light
At high light intensity carbon dioxide becomes the limiting factor, and warm water dissolves more carbon dioxide than cold water, so the 25 °C plant has more of it
The two curves overlap at low light intensity because temperature has no effect on the enzymes of photosynthesis until the water is warmer than about 25 °C
At low light intensity light is the limiting factor at both temperatures; at high light intensity temperature limits the rate, and the enzymes work faster at 25 °C

questions.prompt: In the pondweed investigation, a student places a transparent tank of water between the lamp and the beaker of pondweed. Why?
questions.skill: controlling temperature in the core practical
questions.solution: **To keep the temperature constant.** A lamp gives out heat as well as light, so when it is moved closer the pondweed is warmed as well as lit more brightly. Temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis, so without the tank two variables would change at once and the effect of light intensity could not be separated. The water in the tank absorbs the heat and lets the light through, so only the light intensity changes. The tank does not focus the light, the pondweed is already in water, and the bubbles rise freely whatever is in front of the lamp.

markScheme.description: absorbs heat from the lamp so temperature stays constant and only light intensity changes

options: It focuses the lamp's light onto the pondweed, so the plant receives more light energy at every distance and gives off more bubbles for the student to count
It supplies the extra water that the pondweed needs for photosynthesis when the light intensity is high and the reaction is running fast
It absorbs heat from the lamp, so the temperature of the pondweed stays the same when the lamp is moved closer and only the light intensity changes
It catches the oxygen bubbles as they rise, so they do not gather on the leaves and block the light from reaching the chloroplasts

questions.prompt: Give the name of the green substance in chloroplasts that absorbs the light energy used in photosynthesis.
questions.solution: **Chlorophyll.** Photosynthesis is endothermic: it takes in energy, and that energy is light, absorbed by the green pigment chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts. The absorbed energy drives the reaction of carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen. Chlorophyll is why leaves are green, and why the cells of roots, which have no chloroplasts, cannot photosynthesise.

questions.prompt: Pondweed in a beaker of water is lit by a lamp. The oxygen it gives off is collected in a gas syringe: 1.8 cm³ of oxygen is collected in 12 minutes. Calculate the rate of photosynthesis in cm³ of oxygen per hour.
questions.skill: rate from an oxygen volume and a time
questions.solution: Rate $= \dfrac{\text{volume}}{\text{time}}$. In 12 minutes, 1.8 cm³ was collected, so the rate is $\dfrac{1.8}{12} = 0.15$ cm³ per minute. There are 60 minutes in an hour, so $0.15 \times 60 = 9$ cm³ per hour. (Or: an hour is five lots of 12 minutes, so $1.8 \times 5 = 9$.) Measuring the volume of gas is more reliable than counting bubbles, because bubbles differ in size.

markScheme.description: divides 1.8 by 12 and scales to an hour (×60), or multiplies 1.8 by 5

questions.prompt: With a lamp 15 cm from pondweed, a student counts 32 bubbles per minute. The lamp is moved to 20 cm. The student predicts 24 bubbles per minute, reasoning that 15 cm is three quarters of 20 cm. Light intensity is proportional to 1/d², where d is the distance from the lamp, and light is the limiting factor throughout. Calculate the rate the student should actually predict.
questions.solution: Light intensity $\propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$, and with light limiting the rate is proportional to the light intensity. Moving from 15 cm to 20 cm multiplies the intensity by $\left(\dfrac{15}{20}\right)^2 = \dfrac{225}{400} = 0.5625$, not by $\dfrac{15}{20} = 0.75$. So the predicted rate is $32 \times 0.5625 = 18$ bubbles per minute. (Check with the values of $1/d^2$: $\dfrac{1}{225}$ at 15 cm and $\dfrac{1}{400}$ at 20 cm, and $32 \times \dfrac{225}{400} = 18$.) The student forgot the square: intensity falls with the square of the distance because the light spreads over an area. The rate does fall as the distance rises, an inverse relationship, but because light intensity is proportional to $1/d^2$ the rate is inversely proportional to $d^2$, not to $d$.

markScheme.description: uses rate proportional to 1/d²: the intensity ratio is (15/20)² = 225/400, or 1/225 against 1/400

questions.prompt: In the pondweed investigation, after the lamp is moved to a new distance the student waits two minutes before starting to count bubbles. Explain why.
questions.solution: The rate of photosynthesis does not change the instant the light changes: the pondweed takes time to **adjust to the new light intensity**, and for the first minute or so it is still giving off oxygen at something close to the old rate. Waiting means the count measures the rate **at the new distance** and not a mixture of the two, so the result for each distance is valid.

markScheme.description: the plant takes time to adjust to the new light intensity, so the rate changes gradually
so the count reflects the new distance, not the previous one

criteria.text: Explains that the rate of photosynthesis takes time to adjust to the new light intensity, so for a short while the pondweed is still producing oxygen at close to the old rate
Explains that waiting means the bubbles counted belong to the new distance rather than to a mixture of the old and new rates, so the result for each distance is valid

questions.modelAnswer: When the lamp is moved, the light intensity at the pondweed changes at once, but the rate of photosynthesis does not. The reactions inside the chloroplasts take a little time to speed up or slow down, and oxygen already made is still working its way out of the cut stem, so for a minute or two the bubbles still reflect the old light intensity. If the student counted straight away, the result for the new distance would be a mixture of the two rates and would not be a fair measure of that distance. Waiting two minutes lets the plant settle at its new rate, so each count belongs to the distance it is recorded against.

questions.prompt: In a lake, the total biomass of fish depends on the rate of photosynthesis of the algae, even though the fish do not photosynthesise. Explain why.
questions.skill: producers as the source of biomass
questions.solution: The algae are the lake's **producers**. Photosynthesis uses light energy to make **glucose** from carbon dioxide and water, and the algae use that glucose to build the rest of their **biomass**, so the rate of photosynthesis sets how much algal biomass there is. The fish cannot make their own food: every fish either eats algae or eats animals that ate algae, so **almost all the biomass in the lake's food chains traces back to the algae**. If the algae photosynthesise slowly, there is less biomass to pass along the chains and the lake can support fewer fish.

markScheme.description: algae are producers: photosynthesis makes glucose, from which the algae build their biomass
fish cannot make their own food; they eat algae or animals that ate algae
so the biomass available to pass along the food chains, and hence the fish biomass, is set by the rate of photosynthesis

criteria.text: Explains that the algae are producers: photosynthesis uses light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, and the algae use the glucose to build their biomass
Explains that the fish cannot make their own food, so every fish eats algae or eats animals that ate algae

Concludes that almost all the biomass in the lake's food chains traces back to the algae, so the rate of photosynthesis sets how much biomass can pass along the chains and how many fish the lake can support

questions.modelAnswer: The algae are the producers of the lake. Photosynthesis is the main process in the lake that makes food: it uses light energy to react carbon dioxide and water, producing glucose and oxygen, and the algae then use that glucose, with mineral ions from the water, to make the proteins and other substances that form their biomass. The faster the algae photosynthesise, the more biomass they produce. The fish cannot do any of this. A fish gets its biomass from what it eats, and that is either algae directly or small animals that themselves fed on algae. Whichever route the food takes, almost all the organic matter in the fish began as glucose made by photosynthesis in the algae. So the biomass of the whole lake, including all of its fish, is limited by how much biomass the algae can make, and that is set by their rate of photosynthesis. A shaded or cold lake with slow photosynthesis can support only a small mass of fish, however many eggs the fish lay.

questions.prompt:
A student investigates how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis. She places a lamp at a measured distance d from a beaker of pondweed, waits, and counts the bubbles of oxygen released in one minute. She counts once at each distance.

| Distance d (cm) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubbles per minute | 48 | 12 | 5 | 3 | 2 |

Light intensity is proportional to 1/d². Explain how the student should process and plot her results to test whether the rate of photosynthesis is directly proportional to light intensity, explain what the results show, and explain two improvements to her method.
questions.skill: processing core practical data with the inverse square law
questions.solution: Light intensity cannot be measured directly here, but it is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{d^2}$, so the student should **calculate $1/d^2$ for each distance** (0.01 at 10 cm, 0.0025 at 20 cm, and so on) and **plot rate against $1/d^2$**, not against distance. If the rate is directly proportional to light intensity the points lie on a **straight line through the origin**. The data fit this: doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm cuts $1/d^2$ to a quarter, and the rate falls from 48 to 12, also a quarter; at 30 cm, a ninth of the intensity, the rate is about a ninth, 5. So **light is the limiting factor** across this range: more light energy means a faster reaction and more oxygen. Had the line bent and levelled off at the highest intensities, another factor, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, would have become limiting. Two improvements. The lamp **heats the water** as it is brought closer, so temperature changes as well as light; a tank of water between lamp and beaker, or a thermometer and a check that the temperature is constant, keeps it a fair test. **Bubbles vary in size** and she counted only once; collecting the gas in a syringe or capillary tube and measuring its volume, and repeating each distance three times to take a mean, would make the results more reliable. Working in a darkened room, so background light does not add to the lamp's (which matters most at 50 cm), or adding sodium hydrogencarbonate so carbon dioxide does not run short, are sound improvements too.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the rate falls as the lamp is moved away, or that 1/d² should be calculated, and gives an improvement without saying why it helps

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains that rate should be plotted against 1/d² and that a straight line through the origin shows direct proportion, uses the figures to show the pattern or identifies light as the limiting factor, and gives at least one improvement with its reason

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a complete account: 1/d² calculated and plotted, straight line through the origin as the test, the figures shown to fit (48 to 12 as the intensity quarters), light identified as the limiting factor with what a levelling off would mean, and two valid improvements, each explained

criteria.text: Says that light intensity is proportional to 1/d², so 1/d² should be calculated for each distance and the rate plotted against 1/d² rather than against distance

Explains that direct proportion shows as a straight line through the origin, and that the figures fit: doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm quarters 1/d² and the rate falls from 48 to 12, also a quarter
Explains that light is the limiting factor over this range, because more light energy drives the reaction faster and releases more oxygen
Explains that if the line had bent and levelled off at high light intensity, another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature would have become limiting

Explains one valid improvement with its reason, for example: a tank of water between lamp and beaker, or an LED lamp, so the lamp's heat does not change the temperature; collecting the gas and measuring its volume, because bubbles differ in size; repeating each distance and taking a mean; a darkened room so background light does not add to the lamp's; or sodium hydrogencarbonate in the water so carbon dioxide does not run short
Explains a second, different valid improvement with its reason, from the same range

questions.modelAnswer:
**Processing the results.** The student changed the distance, but the variable that matters is light intensity, and that is proportional to 1/d². So she should calculate 1/d² for every distance: 0.01 at 10 cm, 0.0025 at 20 cm, 0.0011 at 30 cm, 0.000625 at 40 cm and 0.0004 at 50 cm. She then plots rate against 1/d², with 1/d² on the horizontal axis. If the rate is directly proportional to light intensity, the points lie on a straight line that passes through the origin.

**What the results show.** The figures fit that line. Doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm cuts 1/d² to a quarter, and the rate falls from 48 to 12 bubbles per minute, also a quarter. Trebling the distance to 30 cm cuts the intensity to a ninth, and 5 is close to a ninth of 48. So over this range the rate is directly proportional to light intensity: light is the limiting factor, and every increase in light energy drives the reaction faster and releases more oxygen. If the line had bent over and become flat at the highest intensities, light would no longer have been limiting there, and the carbon dioxide concentration or the temperature would have been holding the rate down instead.

**Two improvements.** First, the lamp gives out heat as well as light, so moving it closer warms the water, and temperature affects the rate too. A transparent tank of water between the lamp and the beaker absorbs the heat and lets the light through, or a thermometer in the beaker can confirm the temperature stayed constant. That keeps light intensity the only variable changing. Second, bubbles are not all the same size, so a count is not a measure of volume, and one count per distance means a single odd minute decides the result. Collecting the oxygen in a gas syringe or a capillary tube and measuring its volume gives a true rate, and repeating each distance three times and taking a mean shows up any anomaly and makes the results more reliable.

examTechnique.body: Photosynthesis questions come in three shapes: the equation and where it happens (recall), a graph of rate against a factor to explain (limiting factors), and the core practical to describe, evaluate or process (variables, rates, the inverse square law). Say "limiting factor" by name, say which factor it is on each part of the graph, and give rates with a unit such as bubbles per minute.
examinerErrors: Writing glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water and calling it photosynthesis: that is respiration.
Saying the curve levels off because "the plant cannot photosynthesise any faster" without naming the factor that now limits it.
Treating light intensity as proportional to distance: it is proportional to 1 over distance squared.
Describing the practical without saying what is kept the same, or how.
Giving a rate without a time in it, such as "36 bubbles".
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the limiting factor on every part of a graph, explains a plateau by the factor in shortest supply, handles two curves by saying what is shared and what differs, uses 1/d² correctly in predictions, and evaluates the practical with a specific flaw and a fix that addresses it.
